translation: Water diminished and people left the settlement. No one lived there, and no one remembered why. A woodworker went there and first treated the abandoned place as a thing. The woodworker cut a bounded portion of a house's timber, took it, and made a sound new house. On returning, the woodworker took much more; the old roof split open, and a doorway made from the later timber would not fit. The woodworker returned with a child. Rain entered; water lived in the old house. The child referred to the settlement as PERSON and asked, “Water lives in the old house. Who restores the roof?” The woodworker understood and then also used PERSON reference. The roof and doorway were mended; the roof was restored to the settlement under SOCIAL personhood, hearth-fire was renewed, and the child spoke an old name to the place. The path grew. Thereafter people habitually took only bounded portions while restoring the roof, renewing the hearth, and speaking the old name.
notes: Phase 2a place-personhood folktale regression. The first bounded salvage succeeds; excess causes structural injury. Child-led PERSON reference precedes adult recognition. Physical MEND and relational RESTORE remain lexically distinct, while continued use survives under reciprocal maintenance. The responsive referent remains deliberately ambiguous between settlement, houses collectively, and the relationship constituted through them.
